common_name: Pot-a-peno Pepper (Compact Container Jalapeño, AAS Winner)

planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; Pot-a-peno is an All-America Selections winner bred specifically for container growing, producing a full crop of true jalapeño-flavored peppers on a compact plant well under a foot tall.

directions: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost date and transplant into a large container or garden bed after danger of frost has passed. Pot-a-peno was bred specifically to solve a common problem with growing jalapeños on a patio or balcony — most jalapeño varieties grow too large and sprawling for small containers — by combining a genuinely dwarf, compact plant habit with full-sized, full-flavored jalapeño fruit and strong productivity. It was recognized as an All-America Selections winner for combining container-friendly size with reliable yield and classic jalapeño heat and flavor, unlike many ornamental dwarf peppers bred for looks rather than culinary use. Fruits mature from green to red if left on the plant, with red fruits noticeably sweeter and slightly hotter than green. Because the plant is so compact, it benefits from a slightly richer potting mix and more frequent watering and feeding than an in-ground pepper, since a small root zone dries out and depletes nutrients faster. Harvest fruits at the green stage for classic jalapeño flavor or let them ripen to red for a sweeter, smokier heat, useful for chipotle-style drying.
sources: All-America Selections — Pot-a-peno Pepper award notes
PanAmerican Seed — Compact Container Pepper Breeding

common_name: Candy Corn Pepper (Multicolor Ornamental Hot Pepper)

planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; Candy Corn is an ornamental-edible pepper bred to produce upright, tapered, yellow-to-orange-to-red fruit that resembles the classic autumn candy, providing striking multicolor display alongside genuine culinary use.

directions: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; Candy Corn is compact enough for containers and makes an eye-catching patio or border plant. Bred for its ornamental-edible dual purpose, Candy Corn produces upright clusters of small, tapered fruit that ripen through a sequence from pale yellow at the base through orange to a bright red tip while still on the plant, closely mimicking the look of the classic Halloween candy for which it is named. Fruits carry moderate heat, milder than a typical cayenne but with real chile flavor, and are fully usable fresh, dried, or in hot sauce at any color stage, though flavor and heat both increase slightly as fruit ripens toward red. The compact, well-branched plant holds its colorful fruit upright above the foliage for maximum visual display, making it as valuable in a mixed ornamental border or container planting as in a dedicated vegetable bed. Harvest fruit continuously through the season to encourage more flowering and fruit set.
sources: Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Candy Corn Pepper variety notes

common_name: Green Light Cucumber (Seedless Snacking Cucumber, AAS Winner)

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant after last frost in warm soil; Green Light is an All-America Selections winner bred as a compact, high-yielding, seedless snacking cucumber that produces thin-skinned, burpless mini cucumbers without needing a pollinator, making it well suited to small gardens and containers.

directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep after the danger of frost has passed, or set out transplants, providing a small trellis or cage for the compact vines. Green Light was recognized as an All-America Selections winner for combining parthenocarpic (seedless, self-fruitful) fruit set with a compact plant habit and outstanding yield of crisp, thin-skinned, 4-5 inch mini cucumbers ideal for snacking whole or slicing. Because the plant sets fruit without pollination, it performs reliably even when bee activity is low and produces cucumbers with essentially no seed cavity or bitterness, with skin tender enough that peeling is unnecessary. The compact vines are well suited to small raised beds, large containers, and gardens with limited trellis space, and the plant's dense productivity means frequent picking — every one to two days once fruiting begins — keeps cucumbers at the ideal small size and encourages continued production through the season. Consistent watering during fruit development prevents bitterness and misshapen fruit.

common_name: Diamond Frost Euphorbia (Baby's-Breath-Like Heat-Tolerant Filler Annual)

planting.note: Set out transplants after last frost in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Diamond Frost is a sterile Proven Winners hybrid that blooms nonstop from spring through frost without deadheading, tolerating heat, humidity, and drought far better than the baby's breath and gypsophila it visually resembles.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade after the danger of frost has passed, spacing plants 12-18 inches apart. Diamond Frost is a sterile hybrid euphorbia introduced by Proven Winners that produces a continuous cloud of tiny white bracts resembling baby's breath, but on a plant that is dramatically more heat-, humidity-, and drought-tolerant than true gypsophila, making it far better suited to Gulf South summers. Because it is sterile, it never sets seed and never needs deadheading, so the airy white cloud of bloom continues uninterrupted from spring through the first hard frost with essentially no maintenance beyond routine watering. Its fine texture and neutral white color make it one of the most useful filler plants in mixed containers and borders, softening bold flower colors and foliage the way baby's breath does in a cut-flower arrangement. It tolerates both full sun and part shade, blooming a bit less densely in shadier spots but remaining attractive, and it shrugs off both drought and the occasional overwatering better than most bedding annuals. Shear back lightly if plants become leggy in late summer to refresh density for fall bloom.
sources: Proven Winners — Diamond Frost Euphorbia variety notes

common_name: Dragon's Breath Celosia (Dark Burgundy Foliage Plume Celosia)

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost, or direct sow after soil warms; Dragon's Breath combines nearly black-burgundy foliage with vivid crimson plumes, giving it strong ornamental impact in beds and containers through Gulf South summer heat, which celosia tolerates better than most bedding annuals.

directions: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost, or direct sow once the soil has warmed, and transplant or thin to 10-14 inches apart in full sun. Dragon's Breath is a wheat-type celosia (Celosia spicata) selected for foliage so dark it reads as near-black in most light, providing dramatic contrast for the slender, upright, bright crimson-red flower plumes held above it from midsummer through frost. Unlike many bedding annuals, celosia thrives in the peak heat and humidity of a Gulf Coast summer, often blooming most heavily during the weeks when cooler-season annuals have stalled out, and it tolerates considerable drought once established. The dark foliage makes it a striking foil for silver- or chartreuse-leaved companions, and the flower plumes are excellent both fresh and dried for arrangements, holding color and form well after cutting. Deadhead spent plumes to encourage continued branching and bloom, and stake taller plantings in windy, exposed sites since the flower heads can become top-heavy.
sources: Proven Winners / PanAmerican Seed — Celosia spicata breeding notes
